'''James D. Wuest''' is a Canadian [[chemist]], [[materials scientist]] and academic. He is a professor of [[Chemistry]] at the [[Université de Montréal]],<ref name=aaa>{{Cite web|url=https://chimie.umontreal.ca/english/department-directory/professors/professor/in/in33231/sg/Boutayna%20Rhourri/|title=Professor|website=Département de chimie – Université de Montréal}}</ref> where he teaches and leads a research group.<ref name=www>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wuestgroup.com/jameswuest.html|title=Prof. James D. Wuest|website=www.wuestgroup.com}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Wuest is most known for his contributions to the development of [[modular construction]], using it as a method for creating molecular materials with predictable structures and properties. His research has contributed to information on molecular organization in materials and ways to control it.<ref name=ggg>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.ca/citations?user=hZlpsLwAAAAJ&hl=en|title=Google Scholar–James D. Wuest}}</ref> He is the recipient of the 1988 Merck Sharp & Dohme Award and the 2001 [[Alfred Bader]] Award in Organic Chemistry from the [[Canadian Society for Chemistry]],<ref name=aba>{{Cite web|url=https://cscorgdiv.ca/alfred-bader-award|title=Alfred Bader Award|website=CSC ORG DIV}}</ref> the 1992 [[Rutherford Memorial Medal]] from the [[Royal Society of Canada]],<ref name=rmm>{{Cite web|url=https://rsc-src.ca/en/awards-excellence/past-award-winners|title=Past Award Winners|date=October 21, 2018|website=The Royal Society of Canada}}</ref> the [[American Chemical Society]]'s [[Arthur C. Cope Award|Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award]] in 2005,<ref name=acc>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/funding/awards/arthur-cope-scholar-award/past-recipients.html|title=Past Recipients|website=American Chemical Society}}</ref> the Prix Urgel-Archambault from the [[Association francophone pour le savoir]] in 2008,<ref name=pua>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acfas.ca/prix-concours/prix-acfas/2008/prix-urgel-archambault/james-wuest|title=Prix Acfas Urgel-Archambault – James D. Wuest|website=www.acfas.ca}}</ref> the 2013 [[Prix Marie-Victorin]] from the [[Government of Québec]],<ref name=pmv>{{Cite web|url=https://prixduquebec.gouv.qc.ca/recipiendaires/james-d-wuest/|title=James D. Wuest|date=November 11, 2013|website=Prix du Québec}}</ref> and the 2021 Canadian Light Source T. K. Sham Award in Materials Chemistry.<ref name=cls>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cheminst.ca/awards/csc/sham/|title=Canadian Light Source T. K. Sham Award in Materials Chemistry|website=The Chemical Institute of Canada}}</ref> Additionally, he was awarded a Killam Research Fellowship in 1992 and a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1999.<ref name=guf>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/james-d-wuest/|title=James D. Wuest|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation...}}</ref>

Wuest is a Fellow and Life Member of the Royal Society of Canada.<ref name=rsc>{{Cite web|url=https://rsc-src.ca/en/find-rsc-member/results|title=Member Directory|website=The Royal Society of Canada}}</ref> He was an Editor of the ''[[Canadian Journal of Chemistry]]'' from 1992 to 1997 and has been on the advisory board of ''Materials Chemistry Frontiers'' since 2019.<ref name=mcf>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/journals-books-databases/about-journals/materials-chemistry-frontiers/|title=Materials Chemistry Frontiers journal|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref>

==Education==
Wuest earned a bachelor's degree in [[Chemistry]] and Mathematics from [[Cornell University]] in 1969 and received his PhD in chemistry in 1973 from [[Harvard University]], where he was a [[National Science Foundation]] Fellow and a student of [[Robert Burns Woodward|Robert B. Woodward]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hollisarchives.lib.harvard.edu/repositories/4/archival_objects/1076470|title=Wuest &#124; HOLLIS for}}</ref>

==Career==
Wuest began his academic career as an [[assistant professor]] of chemistry at Harvard University from 1973 to 1979, and he became a Fellow at the [[Harvard Medical School]] in 1980. He joined the Université de Montréal as an associate professor in 1981 and has served as a professor of Chemistry since 1986.<ref name=aaa/> In addition, he directed the Réseau québécois de recherche en synthèse organique from 2002 to 2007. From 2007 to 2014, he served as director of the Major Central Research Facility for the Study of Nanostructured Molecular Materials and held the [[Canada Research Chair]] in Molecular Materials from 2001 to 2022.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://www.nrcresearchpress.com/doi/10.1139/cjc-2020-0179|title=Professor James D. Wuest|first1=Graham|last1=Bodwell|first2=Stephen|last2=Hanessian|date=July 15, 2020|journal=Canadian Journal of Chemistry|volume=98|issue=7|pages=v–vi|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1139/cjc-2020-0179 |bibcode=2020CaJCh..98D...5B |url-access=subscription}}</ref> He has been a member of the Institut Courtois and its Scientific Advisory Board since 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://institut-courtois.umontreal.ca/en/team/james-wuest-2/|title=James Wuest|website=Institut Courtois}}</ref>

==Research==
Wuest's research focuses on molecular materials but spans different areas of science, including [[organic chemistry]], [[inorganic chemistry]], [[physical chemistry]], [[surface science]], and [[computation]]. The work places an emphasis on molecular design, synthesis, structural analysis, and the construction of new materials by controlled molecular association.<ref name=ggg/>

===Modular construction===
Wuest is a pioneer in modular construction, a method for creating predictably ordered materials by using molecular modules that engage in well-defined associations, thereby holding their neighbors in predetermined positions.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00012a057|title=Use of hydrogen bonds to control molecular aggregation. Self-assembly of three-dimensional networks with large chambers|first1=Michel|last1=Simard|first2=Dan|last2=Su|first3=James D.|last3=Wuest|date=June 15, 1991|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=113|issue=12|pages=4696–4698|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/ja00012a057|bibcode=1991JAChS.113.4696S |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/jo00259a037|title=Use of hydrogen bonds to control molecular aggregation. Extensive, self-complementary arrays of donors and acceptors|first1=Yves|last1=Ducharme|first2=James D.|last2=Wuest|date=November 15, 1988|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=53|issue=24|pages=5787–5789|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/jo00259a037|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Surface science===
Wuest's research has shown how modular construction can be used in 2D to help control adsorption on surfaces. His studies have demonstrated the special value of a dual approach in which 3D molecular organization (determined by X-ray diffraction) is compared systematically with 2D organization on surfaces (revealed by [[scanning probe microscopy]]). This approach has provided insights related to molecular organization, such as how crystallization can be inhibited.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja0742535|title=Frustrated 2D Molecular Crystallization|first1=Hui|last1=Zhou|first2=Hung|last2=Dang|first3=Ji-Hyun|last3=Yi|first4=Antonio|last4=Nanci|first5=Alain|last5=Rochefort|first6=James D.|last6=Wuest|date=November 1, 2007|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=129|issue=45|pages=13774–13775|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/ja0742535|pmid=17948995 |bibcode=2007JAChS.12913774Z |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/ES2131684T3/en|title=MODIFICATION OF THE SURFACE OF AN IMPLANT WITH BIOACTIVE CONJUGATES TO IMPROVE ITS INTEGRATION}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5824651A/en|title=Process for modification of implant surface with bioactive conjugates for improved integration}}</ref>

===Molecular crystallization===
Wuest and his research group study aspects of molecular crystallization, such as ways to inhibit crystallization and make amorphous solids, the relationship between crystallization and gelation, and the origins of polymorphism, which is the ability of compounds to have multiple crystalline forms. He has developed new ways to diversify solid forms and optimize products. Furthermore, he and his group have investigated the factors contributing to high levels of polymorphism<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.joc.2c00369|title=Surprising Chemistry of 6-Azidotetrazolo[5,1- a ]phthalazine: What a Purported Natural Product Reveals about the Polymorphism of Explosives|first1=Aaron Gabriel|last1=Nunez Avila|first2=Benoît|last2=Deschênes-Simard|first3=Joseph E.|last3=Arnold|first4=Mathieu|last4=Morency|first5=Daniel|last5=Chartrand|first6=Thierry|last6=Maris|first7=Gilles|last7=Berger|first8=Graeme M.|last8=Day|first9=Stephen|last9=Hanessian|first10=James D.|last10=Wuest|date=May 20, 2022|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=87|issue=10|pages=6680–6694|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/acs.joc.2c00369|pmid=35504046 |hdl=2013/ULB-DIPOT:oai:dipot.ulb.ac.be:2013/344310|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.accounts.0c00511|title=Phosphangulene: A Molecule for All Chemists|first1=Alice|last1=Heskia|first2=Thierry|last2=Maris|first3=James D.|last3=Wuest|date=October 20, 2020|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|volume=53|issue=10|pages=2472–2482|via=CrossRef|doi=10.1021/acs.accounts.0c00511|pmid=33026221 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.cgd.9b00907|title=Foiling Normal Patterns of Crystallization by Design. In this work, Wuest and his research group have used an approach that combines database mining, computational analysis, and experimentation as a way to understand the rules of crystallization, expand the range of known molecular behavior, and find new crystalline materials.<ref name=sss/>

===Sustainable organic-based batteries and devices===
Wuest and his research group have used their approach to develop organic materials suitable for batteries and other devices. They have reviewed various aspects of the field<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2013/cs/c3cs35447d|title=Using volatile additives to alter the morphology and performance of active layers in thin-film molecular photovoltaic devices incorporating bulk heterojunctions|first1=Minh Trung|last1=Dang|first2=James D.|last2=Wuest|date=November 4, 2013|journal=Chemical Society Reviews|volume=42|issue=23|pages=9105–9126|via=pubs.rsc.org|doi=10.1039/C3CS35447D|pmid=24005234 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/cr300005u|title=Controlling the Morphology and Performance of Bulk Heterojunctions in Solar Cells. *1992 – Rutherford Memorial Medal, Royal Society of Canada<ref name=rmm/>
*1996 – Elected Fellow, Royal Society of Canada<ref name=rsc/>
*1999 – Guggenheim Fellowship, John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation<ref name=guf/>
*2001 – Alfred Bader Award in Organic Chemistry, Canadian Society for Chemistry<ref name=aba/>
*2005 – Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award, American Chemical Society<ref name=acc/>

*2021 – Canadian Light Source T. K. Sham Award in Materials Chemistry, Chemical Institute of Canada<ref name=cls/>
